hook_text: Open any new car door and almost nothing you touch is metal. Here is why, and where it all goes.
clip_script: A modern car is a tenth plastic by weight, a fifth by volume, 150 kilograms in two hundred parts. Why: lighter saves fuel, moulds into any shape, never rusts, softer in a crash. Where: polypropylene bumpers that spring back, polycarbonate lamp lenses that do not shatter, a dashboard of plastic skin over foam, a blow-moulded HDPE fuel tank that fits round the axle, glass-filled nylon under the bonnet for the heat, PVC on every wire. Steel stays where the loads are: body, chassis, engine. The catch comes at the scrapyard: the steel recycles easily, the plastic is a dozen polymers painted and glued, so most goes to landfill. New cars mark every part, clip instead of glue, use fewer plastics. Design for the whole life, including the end.
visual_style: Whiteboard car outline with parts lit up and labelled one by one; a fuel bar shrinking; a scrapyard with a magnet lifting steel and a pile of mixed plastic; a bumper with a polymer code stamp.
mood: Showroom walk-around with a mechanic's honesty.
pacing: Share, why, outside, inside, underneath, steel, end of life.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and find the polymer code moulded on the inside of a car bumper or a plastic trim piece.
